papers.title: A multi-tissue transcriptome strategy for genomic resource development in Pinus edulis
papers.abstract: Premise:: Conifers comprise one-sixth of global forests and landscape genomic studies are urgently needed to understand their biology, yet relatively few conifer species have reference genomes. Targeted exon-capture is a practical alternative to whole-genome sequencing, but selecting loci without a reference genome remains a barrier. We developed a multi-tissue reference transcriptome for pi non pine (Pinus edulis) to ask how multi-tissue sampling improves probe design, and what is lost under a conventional single-tissue approach. Methods: We assembled a reference transcriptome from four diploid tissues (needle, phloem, root, vegetative bud) and one haploid tissue (megagametophyte), using the latter as a pseudo-guide. We designed a target-capture probe-set by prioritizing highly expressed P. edulis transcripts and transcripts matching a conifer exon database. Results: We recovered 76% of conserved plant genes with few duplicated transcripts. Filtering yielded 15,664 transcripts totaling 31.4 Mb, ~0.1% of the genome. Tissue-specific expression was substantial: 27.4% of transcripts occurred exclusively in non-needle tissues. Functional annotation confirmed complementary contributions, including seed-desiccation and germination genes from megagametophytes, and defense- and stress-associated genes from roots and phloem. Discussion: We built a transcriptome and efficient probe set using a roadmap suitable for other non-model plants with large genomes; keys to success were prioritizing complementary tissues and using expression-based filtering.

papers.title: Transcriptional perturbation effects remain structured beyond the leading global trend
papers.abstract: Prior work has described a global transcriptional response to gene perturbation, with many perturbations moving cells along a common direction. We find that perturbations contribute differently to this leading global trend and that substantial organization remains beyond it, including transferable perturbation-specific effects across datasets and a common hierarchy of responsive genes across perturbations. These patterns make simple strategies surprisingly competitive even in predicting effects beyond the leading global component.

papers.title: Gene-environment interaction loci with signatures of mid- to late Holocene selection show evidence for diet-dependent genetic effects
papers.abstract: Environmental change is a major driver of adaptation, yet most evolutionary studies assume that genetic effects remain constant across environments. Recent biobank-scale studies have identified widespread gene-environment interactions (GxE), but their contribution to recent human evolution remains unclear. Here, we combined genome-wide GxE maps with allele-frequency trajectories spanning the last ~10,000 years to test whether environmentally responsive variants contributed to recent human adaptation. Among 45 independent loci, three showed significant signatures of directional selection. These loci, associated with urate, LDL-C and cholesterol levels, showed parallel frequency increases and overlapping acceleration points around 4,700-7,200 years ago. Selection-associated GxE loci were enriched for urate-related variants and for interactions involving meat and cheese consumption. Diet-associated variants showed a consistent interaction direction across loci. Notably, across candidate traits, GxE variants were enriched among significant GWAS loci with selection signatures. Furthermore, analyses across worldwide populations revealed broadly shared derived allele frequency increases and comparable temporal patterns. Taken together, our results suggest that gene-environment interactions present an important and previously underappreciated component of recent human evolution.

papers.title: A Unified Comparison of 10X Genomics and Parse Biosciences scRNA-seq Technologies
papers.abstract: Droplet-based and split-pool barcoding are the two dominant high-throughput single-cell RNA-seq paradigms, yet their systematic biases remain incompletely characterized. We compared seven matched 10X Genomics Chromium and Parse Biosciences Evercode WT sample pairs from five studies spanning multiple tissues and species focusing on gene counts and compositional differences rather than cell-type resolution. By separating Parse reads by priming strategy, we distinguished biases arising from priming chemistry from platform-level effects. These effects were largely independent, with platform-level differences substantially larger. Priming strategy introduced a GC-content bias within Parse, whereas the two platforms showed a consistent compositional shift across priming strategies, supported by differential capture of nuclear- and cytoplasmic-enriched transcripts. We interpret this shift as a relative enrichment of nuclear RNA in Parse. Finally, using contamination measures that do not assume a droplet-specific model, we found background RNA contamination in Parse to be comparable in magnitude to that in 10X, contrary to claims of substantially lower contamination. Together, these results indicate that expression measurements and cell-type composition are not directly interchangeable between the two platforms.

papers.title: Structural variants from donor-specific assemblies affect recurrent chromatin contact divergence in humans
papers.abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are a major source of human genetic diversity, yet their contribution to three-dimensional (3D) genome organization remains difficult to resolve using a standard reference genome. Here, we integrate haplotype-resolved chromatin interaction maps across 354 human and 12 nonhuman ape haplotypes with matched genome assemblies and long-read transcriptomes to determine how inherited SVs influence chromatin organization. We observe significant improvements in contact mapping, with 13.2% of cis Hi-C contacts showing >25 kbp changes in inferred genomic separation and an additional 2.8% of valid contact pairs recovered when using donor-specific assemblies instead of standard references. We show that haplotype-specific chromatin differences are highly selective rather than pervasive, concentrating within 1,790 recurrent contact difference hotspots associated with a restricted subset of SVs. We identified 2,495 chromatin-structure-associated SVs that are enriched in regulatory genomic contexts and are linked to expression variation. Notably, more than 90% of these SVs are derived in the human lineage, consistent with recent remodeling of regulatory architecture at the population level. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating haplotype diversity from pangenomes into studies of chromatin organization and provide a framework for understanding how inherited genomic differences are linked to functional consequences across populations and evolution.

papers.title: Forecasting next-year change in antimicrobial resistance genes in Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii from genomic surveillance data
papers.abstract: Background: Surveillance tells laboratories which antimicrobial resistance genes are circulating now, but not which will change next. We built a model that forecasts, for each resistance gene and year, whether the following year brings a previously unseen allele (sequence variant), called emergence, or a change in the most common allele, called turnover. We tested it separately in Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii. Results: We used genomes annotated with AMRFinderPlus: 2,385 gene-years across 331 genes for K.pneumoniae and 1,059 across 216 for A. baumannii. To remove the effect of sequencing effort, each gene-year was sampled to 10 records and the analysis repeated 25 times. Models were trained on earlier years and tested on later ones, and on genes held out of training. On later years every model ranked genes by risk better than simple baselines in both organisms, and results for held-out genes were close. In K.pneumoniae, turnover was predicted better than emergence (best area under the ROC curve, AUROC, 0.909 versus 0.819). In A. baumannii the order reversed (emergence 0.789, turnover 0.722). The two events also relied on different features. Emergence depended mainly on how many alleles a gene had already accumulated, in both organisms. Turnover in K. pneumoniae depended mainly on how dominant the leading allele already was, and a stability index added a small gain. In A. baumannii it was spread across many weaker features. There, 56% of changes in the leading allele involved only alleles already seen, against 23% in K. pneumoniae, which may make them harder to predict. Conclusions: Changes in resistance genes can be forecast a year ahead from routine genomic surveillance data, including for genes the model has not seen. How well it works, and what it depends on, differs between organisms, so models should be built and validated for each organism, not assumed to transfer. Such models could help laboratories decide which resistance genes to monitor most closely. Keywords: antimicrobial resistance; genomic surveillance; forecasting; machine learning; allele dynamics; Klebsiella pneumoniae; Acinetobacter baumannii

papers.title: A unified framework for quantitative splicing and transcript prediction
papers.abstract: RNA splicing is frequently disrupted by genetic variation, contributing to a wide range of human diseases. Identifying the variants responsible for altered splicing is therefore crucial but has long been challenging. Deep learning models that predict splicing from genomic sequence have substantially advanced their detection, but accurately resolving their quantitative effects on splicing and the resulting transcripts remains an unmet need. Here we introduce SpliceAI2, a deep learning model trained end-to-end on splice site, splice junction, and transcript usage across multiple mammalian species. SpliceAI2 reconstructs complete transcripts directly from genomic sequence and considerably improves identification of splice-altering variants and quantification of their effects in diverse benchmarks spanning cryptic splicing, splicing quantitative trait loci, and massively parallel reporter assays. Human population datasets provide independent validation of these predicted functional effects through evidence of natural selection and associated changes in plasma protein abundance. Application to a rare disease cohort reveals that predicted splice-altering variants are highly enriched in disease-associated genes and account for 15% of the excess genetic burden, with approximately half residing in deep intronic regions likely missed by exome sequencing. Together, these findings establish SpliceAI2 as a major step forward in interpreting splice-altering variants across the human genome.

papers.title: A Plasmid-Derived Machinery Drives Chromosomal Replication Initiation in the Colorectal Cancer-Associated Bacterium Fusobacterium nucleatum and Its Close Relatives
papers.abstract: Chromosome replication initiation in bacterial genomes typically occurs at a single origin, called oriC, through the binding of the DnaA initiator protein to specific chromosomal repeats known as DnaA-boxes. Here, relying on comparative genomics, we show that the family Fusobacteriaceae, which belongs to the order Fusobacteriales alongside the family Leptotrichiaceae, deviates from this paradigm. Our analysis revealed a stark contrast between the two lineages: while dnaA flanks oriC in Leptotrichiaceae, it is notably missing from Fusobacteriaceae genomes. Adjacent to oriC in Fusobacteriaceae, we identified a gene encoding replication initiator protein A (RPA). We characterized RPA as a Rep-type initiator involved in plasmid replication that likely originated from an iteron-containing plasmid, iterons being the plasmid analogues of DnaA-boxes. Phylogenetic reconstruction indicates that the gene encoding RPA was acquired together with its associated iterons and subsequently domesticated by the Fusobacteriaceae ancestor, successfully displacing the ancestral chromosomal dnaA gene at the origin of replication. This shift to a plasmid-derived replication system may represent an adaptive trait of the Fusobacteriaceae, potentially offering new insights into the biology of Fusobacterium nucleatum, a member of this family known to be a major driver of colorectal cancer progression within the tumor microenvironment.

papers.title: Massively scaled variant effect mapping across the MAPK pathway reveals the importance of molecular and cellular context
papers.abstract: Variation alters inherent protein properties like thermodynamic stability and catalytic activity, and these intrinsic effects are shaped by the complex cellular environment. Signaling cascades typify this complexity, with tens or hundreds of proteins acting in concert through regulated states and interactions to transduce signals. Here, we measure the effect of 186,676 variants across 17 proteins in the RAS-MAPK pathway on protein abundance and pathway activity in human cells under diverse conditions, for a total of 503,099 variant effect measurements. We discovered 14,412 dominant negative variants across 12 proteins, nearly all previously unknown, that disrupt specific domains or interaction interfaces while leaving other functions intact and that are depleted from the human population. Measuring the abundance of 106,642 variants across 10 proteins under HSP90 inhibition showed that HSP90 shapes the effect of 67% of missense variants across the pathway, buffering destabilizing variants in both strong and weak clients. Our variant effect data, collected in the context of an intact proteome, enabled us to assess the functional importance of 395 experimentally and computationally modeled MAPK protein interactions. Using additional mutational scans, we resolved how the promiscuous switch II helix binding surface of KRAS accommodates overlapping interactions with LZTR1 and SOS1, revealing distinct allosteric networks that support each interaction. Thus, we establish a framework for measuring variant effects at unprecedented scale in human cells, illuminating fundamental MAPK pathway signaling mechanisms and demonstrating that cellular context profoundly shapes the effect of most variants.

papers.title: BoNTax: a curated genome-based framework for taxonomic classification and characterization of Clostridium botulinum Group I and Clostridium sporogenes
papers.abstract: Clostridium botulinum Group I and Clostridium sporogenes are closely related genomic lineages for which historical toxin-based nomenclature can obscure species-level relationships. We developed BoNTax, a curated taxonomy-first framework that separates average nucleotide identity (ANI)-based species assignment from botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) characterization while integrating assembly quality assessment, multilocus sequence typing (MLST), AMRFinderPlus-based detection of bont genes, other virulence-associated genes, and antimicrobial resistance genes into standardized outputs. Analysis of 966 genomes informed genome-size criteria and the selection of 46 representative references comprising 22 C. botulinum Group I and 24 C. sporogenes genomes. Pairwise ANI resolved these references into two distinct species clusters: within-species ANI values were >95%, whereas between-species values were <95%, supporting a 95% species-level assignment threshold. BoNTax was implemented in GalaxyTrakr as complementary FASTQ- and FASTA-input workflows that converge on a common downstream analysis. The workflow completed analysis of all 42 validation genomes. Among the 32 genomes with a reported taxonomic identity, 29 assignments were concordant and three prompted taxonomic re-evaluations. For the ten genomes reported as taxonomically unknown, BoNTax provided ANI-based assignments. Of the three discordances, BT-22100019 was assigned to C. sporogenes rather than the reported C. botulinum Group I, whereas R1125/03 and R1135/03 showed 99.96% ANI to C. caseinilyticum DSM 46279, supporting their identification as C. caseinilyticum. MLST assignments were concordant for genomes with established profiles except PNUSAB000061, for which ST183 was not assigned by the MLST database version used in this analysis. BoNT type and subtype detection was fully concordant across toxigenic genomes, including bivalent strains. Thirty-one genomes met the predefined assembly-size QC criterion, whereas 11 received QC warnings, including all eight datasets representing four known mixed cultures. BoNTax therefore provides a reproducible genomic framework for resolving closely related clostridial lineages, identifying taxonomic annotations requiring re-evaluation, and reporting clinically relevant toxin information without conflating toxin genotype with species identity.

papers.title: Disrupted chromatin architecture blocks B lymphopoiesis in Down syndrome
papers.abstract: Human fetal haematopoiesis requires developmental potential to be encoded before lineage identity becomes transcriptionally apparent, but whether three-dimensional genome architecture provides such information is unknown. Here we develop ChromE-seq, a scalable single-cell assay that jointly profiles chromatin conformation and transcription, and integrate it with chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation to generate a multimodal atlas of ~400,000 haematopoietic cells from disomic and trisomy 21 (T21) human fetal liver. Chromatin contacts frequently preceded lineage-specific transcription or persisted after transcription declined, revealing 3D chromatin priming and memory. Unexpectedly, B-lineage and erythroid differentiation followed opposing architectural trajectories, with progressive loss and gain of chromatin connectivity, respectively. T21 disproportionately disrupted B-lineage architecture, redistributed interactions towards shorter genomic distances and weakened an EBF1-centred regulatory circuit. Deletion of a T21-sensitive EBF1 loop anchor reproduced the CLP-to-B-progenitor bottleneck observed in T21. These findings establish 3D genome architecture as an organizing layer of human fetal haematopoiesis that links developmental potential with lineage-specific vulnerability to genomic perturbation.

papers.title: Gene functional-state covariance reveals modular structure in the Arabidopsis thaliana dispensable genome
papers.abstract: Classical multilocus theory predicts that selection acting on combinations of loci can maintain non-random associations among allelic states, causing selection to act on multilocus genotypes rather than individual alleles. Across eukaryotic species, pangenome studies have documented thousands of genes that vary in functional status between individuals, yet this variation is analyzed as if each gene evolves independently. Here we test for non-random association within the dispensable pangenome across 1,012 natural genotypes of Arabidopsis thaliana to better understand the structure and evolution of eukaryotic pangenomes. Genome-wide pairwise association testing of loss-of-function alleles across genotypes identified 150,033 significantly covarying gene pairs among 5,679 unique genes after controlling for kinship and population structure. Most associations were between genes on different chromosomes, and covarying gene pairs showed greater co-expression and functional similarity than expected by chance. Network analysis revealed a non-random higher-order architecture comprising stable functional communities with distinct biological functions and structured connectivity among communities. The enriched functions and connectivity of communities revealed a tight coupling of modules involving plant immunity, environmental response, and specialized metabolism, highlighting how these systems integrate and evolve in response to dynamic ecological pressures. Taken together, these results show that the dispensable genome has a complex higher-order structure driven by functionally interacting genes, and that variation in gene content provides a population-scale resource for investigating the organization and evolution of biological systems.

papers.title: Genome assemblies and annotations of the poneroid ants Platythyrea mocquerysi (Ponerinae) and Stigmatomma oregonense (Amblyoponinae)
papers.abstract: We present draft genome assemblies for two poneroid ant species with distinctive life history traits: Platythyrea mocquerysi Emery, 1899 (Ponerinae) and Stigmatomma oregonense Wheeler, 1915 (Amblyoponinae). Platythyrea mocquerysi is a Malagasy ant in which larvae produce secretions from a ventral tubercle that are consumed by adults, representing an unusual form of larva-to-adult trophallaxis. Stigmatomma oregonense, a North American "dracula ant," feeds non-lethally on larval haemolymph. Using PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing, we assembled the P. mocquerysi genome (187 Mb, 307 scaffolds, N50 = 5.26 Mb, BUSCO 99.2% complete) and the S. oregonense genome (262 Mb, 1,189 scaffolds, N50 = 0.84 Mb, BUSCO 98.3% complete). These genomes encode 10,860 and 12,354 protein-coding genes, respectively. Repeat content is higher in S. oregonense than in P. mocquerysi, 54.3% against a lower bound of 15.7%. Most of the difference is in unclassified repeats, which we show to be diverged transposable elements. Comparative analysis with two additional poneroid genomes from closely related species reveals that genome size variation across poneroid ants is largely explained by transposable element dynamics, with notable expansions in several gene families including carboxylesterases, serine proteases, and lipid metabolism genes in Amblyoponinae. These genomes provide essential resources for investigating the molecular basis of unconventional brood management strategies in ants.

papers.title: Ayahuasca plant genomes reveal retrotransposon-derived centromeres and contrasting routes to DMT and β-carbolines
papers.abstract: Ayahuasca, used religiously for centuries by Amazonian Indigenous peoples and increasingly studied for its therapeutic potential, owes its psychoactivity to two plants: Psychotria viridis supplies N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT), whereas Banisteriopsis caapi supplies beta-carbolines that render DMT orally active. Here we show that the two plants have distinct genome histories: P. viridis is hexaploid (2n = 6x = 66), consistent with autopolyploidy, and B. caapi is diploid (2n = 2x = 20). CENH3-bound regions of both species are nonetheless enriched in CRM-type Ty3/Gypsy retrotransposons, with additional LINE elements and CRM-derived satellites in B. caapi. In P. viridis, a single multifunctional methyltransferase catalyzes both N-methylations of tryptamine to DMT. In B. caapi, beta-carboline biosynthesis combines dedicated enzymes with an acetaldehyde-dependent Pictet-Spengler cyclization that can proceed non-enzymatically, followed by enantioselective oxidation to harmaline. These resources link the ethnobotanical history of ayahuasca to its molecular basis, providing genomes of both source plants, the genetic structure of traditionally recognized cultivated varieties, and the enzymes behind the alkaloids long combined in this decoction.

papers.title: From APTs to advanced persistent biological threats (APBTs): a taxonomy and large-scale metadata audit of genomic surveillance infrastructure
papers.abstract: Open genomic repositories have become critical infrastructure for pathogen surveillance, variant tracking, outbreak reconstruction, and public health decision making. However, many of these repositories were designed to support rapid scientific data sharing rather than adversarial verification, creating potential security gaps. This paper introduces Advanced Persistent Biological Threats (APBTs), as a framework for understanding how malicious cyber biological actors can gradually disrupt genomic surveillance without entering a laboratory or releasing a biological agent. Instead of altering biological material, an attacker targets the sequence data, metadata, reference datasets, and analytical models used by surveillance systems. We present, to our knowledge, the first integrated multilayer taxonomy of APBTs, structured around a four phase lifecycle, and investigate whether the metadata weaknesses identified by this framework are present in an operational genomic repository. To assess this, we audited 100,000 SARS-CoV-2 BioSample records obtained from the NCBI. A framework of 23 checks was applied across five metadata layers: temporal, geographic, host and specimen, provenance, and technical metadata. Every record triggered at least one APBT relevant metadata vulnerability indicator, with a mean of 7.34 indicators per record (SD = 1.34). Overall, 97.3% of records were classified in the High or Critical severity categories. Every record also contained at least one indicator in both the provenance and technical metadata layers. These results largely reflect the optional status of several fields in the current BioSample submission model rather than isolated errors by individual data contributors. Temporal and geographic information was comparatively complete, while fields needed for provenance reconstruction, chain of custody assessment, technical validation, and analytical interpretation were frequently missing. These findings do not indicate deliberate manipulation. However, the structural incompleteness of BioSample metadata creates vulnerabilities that an adversary can exploit to introduce poisoned, misleading, or weakly traceable metadata into genomic repositories. As a result, maliciously altered metadata can appear plausible, remain undetected, and influence downstream genomic analysis and surveillance. The findings therefore show that widely used pathogen genomic repositories already contain structural weaknesses that can support metadata poisoning as part of an APBT operation.

papers.title: Genome sequence data of Ascogaster reticulata (Hymenoptera: Braconidae)
papers.abstract: Parasitoid wasps develop in or on other arthropods and have evolved a wide range of strategies for exploiting their hosts. Ascogaster reticulata is a solitary egg to larval endoparasitoid wasp belonging to the subfamily Cheloninae of Braconidae. We constructed a genome assembly using long-read sequence data. The assembled genome was 280.5 Mbp, consisting of 209 contigs. The N50 value and GC content ratio were 13.9 Mbp and 30.43%, respectively. The percentage of transposable elements and repetitive regions was 52.43%. The predicted number of genes is 27,261. Merqury revealed that the QV value and completeness of the genome were 61.79 and 99.3917%, respectively. BUSCO analysis detected approximately 99% of the core genes. These results suggest that the genome data were of sufficient quality for use as a reference genome. Therefore, these data can be utilized as a genomic resource for comparative studies within Braconidae and for future investigations into the biology and evolution of Cheloninae parasitoid wasps.

papers.title: Goat genome assemblies, nine breeds for pangenome contribution
papers.abstract: The goat research community benefits from one of the most comprehensive livestock genome assemblies, ARS1. However, the rich diversity of goat breeds suggests that a single individual genome is not enough to represent the species full genomic content. Third-generation sequencing technologies have recently made it possible to generate very high quality assemblies that should enable to elucidate unique and/or complex phenotype determinisms depending on genetic structural variations. In the SeqOccin project, nine goat breeds were selected to represent French goat genetic diversity: Alpine, Boer, Creole, Fosses, Poitevine, Provencale, Pyreneenne, Rove and Saanen. High-molecular-weight DNA was extracted from blood samples and subjected to long read whole-genome sequencing. There reads were used to generate de novo assemblies and were aligned onto the public reference to call structural variants. PacBio HiFi and parental Illumina reads were used to assemble phased haplotypes of the Alpine breed. For the other breeds, PacBio raw (CLR) or ONT reads were generated. Our work demonstrates the feasibility of assembling genomes with a reasonable amount of data and appropriate software packages, delivering one high-quality assembly and 8 standard goat assemblies that pave the way for pangenome construction and structural variant functional studies.

papers.title: Cellular and molecular census of the pleiotropic disease locus Negr1 in zebrafish
papers.abstract: A major challenge in precision medicine is to understand the cellular origin of disease-causing genetic alterations. One prominent example is the Negr1 locus, where common non-coding variants are associated with an unusually broad range of human traits and conditions, including body mass index (BMI), major depression, schizophrenia, autism-spectrum conditions and anorexia. Yet, no coding loss-of-function allele has been established as causal. These observations suggest that distinct Negr1-expressing cell populations underlie distinct traits. However, this hypothesis is difficult to test in tractable experimental systems without first determining where this gene may act. To overcome this limitation, we generated a knock-in reporter at the zebrafish Negr1 locus and combined single-cell transcriptomics with whole-brain registration and single-neuron projection mapping. We found that Negr1 is expressed in a graded manner across neuronal classes of the brain and retina, radial glia and astrocyte-like cells, and most consistently in oligodendrocyte progenitor cells. Projection mapping suggests three conserved hubs formed by olfactory bulb projection neurons, tectal periventricular projection neurons and cerebellar eurydendroid cells. Our findings are consistent with the idea that Negr1 pleiotropy arises from dose perturbation of a rather broadly expressed gene. More generally, this integrative approach to produce granular multimodal datasets should enable high-resolution etiological studies in models of human disease.

papers.title: Contrasting gene gain and loss shape metabolic diversification in the Ralstonia solanacearum species complex
papers.abstract: Metabolic repertoires are continually remodeled by gene acquisition and loss, but how these contrasting processes jointly generate phenotypic diversity within bacterial species complexes remains poorly understood. Here, we elucidated the genetic and evolutionary basis of the classical biovar phenotypes of the Ralstonia solanacearum species complex (RSSC), which are defined by differential utilization of three hexitols (sorbitol, mannitol, and dulcitol) and three disaccharides (lactose, maltose, and cellobiose). Although this classification has been used for over half a century, the genetic determinants and evolutionary origins of these phenotypes have not been systematically resolved. Machine-learning analysis of genomic data from 250 RSSC strains with documented biovar phenotypes, combined with genome-wide association analysis and gene deletion, identified the smoEFGK gene cluster and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)-dependent glucose dehydrogenase (FADGDH) as the major determinants of hexitol and disaccharide utilization, respectively. Comparative phylogenomics revealed fundamentally different evolutionary histories of these loci. An ancestral smoEFGK system was lost early in RSSC evolution and subsequently reacquired by the ancestor of phylotype I through horizontal transfer from a Burkholderia-related lineage, whereas vertically inherited FADGDH underwent recurrent, independent losses across multiple RSSC lineages. Extending the analysis to 1,082 RSSC strains further showed that disaccharide-utilization capacity was significantly depleted among monocot-associated strains after accounting for phylogenetic relatedness and geographic origin. Together, these findings reveal how contrasting trajectories of gene gain and loss can reshape bacterial metabolic repertoires, generate lineage-associated phenotypic diversity, and potentially contribute to ecological differentiation.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal AI modeling of gene regulation and variant effects in the developing human brain
papers.abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation in the developing human brain remains a central challenge in neuroscience, particularly in transient cell types and developmental stages where data are limited. We present Seal, an interpretable AI transfer learning framework for genome-based modeling of gene expression and variant effects with spatiotemporal resolution across 26 brain regions, 30 cell types, and seven developmental stages. Seal predictions enable characterization of both germline and somatic brain variants, and provide mechanistic interpretation by linking sequence variants to transcriptional regulators in spatiotemporal context. Applying Seal to genome-wide association studies, we identify cell types and developmental windows relevant to neuropsychiatric disease risk, revealing shared and distinct regulatory architectures across six neuropsychiatric conditions that align with clinical trajectories. In the Simons Simplex Collection autism cohort whole genome data, Seal uncovers a significant burden of de novo regulatory variants in transient fetal excitatory neurons, revealing a cell-type and developmentally specific regulatory burden. By connecting genetic variation to spatiotemporal regulatory programs, Seal offers a general framework for uncovering mechanisms of human brain development and disease.

papers.title: An improved Trypanosoma vivax genome assembly confirms the distinct organisation of its variant antigen repertoire
papers.abstract: Trypanosoma vivax is a unicellular parasite spread by biting flies and an important livestock pathogen across sub-Saharan Africa and South America. Alongside its better known relative, T. brucei, it causes animal trypanosomosis. An accurate genome sequence is essential to functional genetics as well as the design of novel diagnostics, drugs and vaccines. However, the existing T. vivax genome sequence is fragmentary, making it difficult to examine genomic features such as the Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG) genes that are the basis for antigenic variation, a key phenotype that underpins immune evasion by African trypanosomes. Our aim was to produce a T. vivax genome sequence with improved contiguity to properly characterise the VSG genes. We present a new core genome assembly in 23 scaffolds, forming approximately 10 chromosomes. Many scaffolds are articulated with extensive sub-telomeric domains that, like T. brucei, contain VSG gene arrays but in T. vivax these are near-perfect repeats of intact genes. Using transcriptomic and proteomic analysis of VSG expression during bloodstream infection we show that the active VSG is expressed from a sub-telomeric array while other arrays are silent. We find no evidence for a VSG expression site at the telomeres or elsewhere. Therefore, although monoallelic expression and antigenic switching occur in T. vivax, the familiar regulatory mechanism of T. brucei does not exist in T. vivax. This improved T. vivax genome assembly demonstrates that T. brucei is a poor guide for T. vivax genetics generally and for regulation of antigenic variation specifically.

papers.title: Exploring protein duplication across Archaea genomes
papers.abstract: Gene duplication is a major driver of genomic innovation, but whether paralog accumulation scales uniformly with increasing genome size across the domain Archaea remains unclear. This study presents a domain-wide analysis of 1,829 archaeal genomes and their predicted proteomes to evaluate protein family expansions, their distribution, and lineage-specific patterns of gene duplication. Protein family expansions were classified as recent (90% sequence identity), intermediate (70%), or old (40%) duplications based on sequence-identity thresholds within each family. The findings show that gene duplication content is decoupled from overall proteome size at high sequence-identity levels, indicating that recent paralog retention does not correlate with proteome expansion. Archaeal lineages exhibit contrasting gene duplication profiles. All 1,829 genomes contained paralogs at the 40% sequence identity threshold, indicating the widespread presence of ancient or divergent duplication events. In contrast, paralogs detected at the 90% identity threshold, showed substantial variation across lineages. Their proportion reached up to 16.6% in groups such as Halobacteria, whereas only 74 genomes (4.04%) completely lacked paralogs at this threshold. Highly duplicated families are enriched for membrane transport systems (ABC/MFS), central metabolic enzymes (e.g., acetyl-CoA synthetase), a high proportion of uncharacterized functions, and mobile elements, predominantly transposases. Notably, we identified 314 transposase protein families in Archaea, distributed in 161 unique families in Archaea and 153 families shared with Bacteria, suggesting mechanisms of interdomain gene transfer. Overall, paralog accumulation in Archaea is a lineage-specific phenomenon shaped by targeted functional duplications and mobile element activity, rather than a simple consequence of proteome growth.

papers.title: Living representatives of the spiralian ancestral karyotype revealed by two Lima genomes
papers.abstract: Conserved synteny enables the reconstruction of ancestral chromosome organization across deeply diverged lineages, as demonstrated across metazoans. In Spiralia, comparative genomic analyses have suggested an ancestral karyotype comprising 20 chromosomes. We report high-quality genome assemblies for two Lima species (Lima caribaea and Lima lima) with 20 chromosomes and show that their chromosome organization matches this ancestral state, including four previously described fusion-with-mixing events. Interestingly, other Limidae genus did not retain the ancestral karyotype: they have undergone subsequent lineage-specific fusions. The conserved organization of Lima chromosomes provides a rare genomic anchor for reconstructing ancestral chromosome organization and lineage-specific chromosome evolution across Spiralia and, more broadly, Metazoa.

papers.title: The Genetic Landscape of Structural Variants in Aspergillus flavus using ONT and PacBio Sequencing
papers.abstract: Genetic rearrangement in the absence of selection is poorly understood. Long-read, high-depth sequencing has enabled analysis of the genetic landscape of spontaneous structural variants. We have applied PacBio Revio sequencing to identify the major classes of genetic alterations during long-term vegetative growth in Aspergillus flavus. These classes include a) precise deletions frequently associated with the flanking region of homology, b) clusters of short deletions that are heavily enriched within centromeric and subtelomeric regions that are typically 94% A+T, and c) deletions and expansions within a subset of homopolymer tracts. We find 70 homopolymer tracts longer than 44 bp, dispersed throughout the genome in noncoding regions and unassociated with transposable elements. A broader analysis of third-generation sequenced datasets from fungi found within the Phylum Ascomycota showed a high but variable prevalence of homopolymeric tracts across species. The adventitious identification of a putative flbA mutation, responsible for an altered conidial phenotype, by the Deep Variant AI system also demonstrates the power of this approach. These studies show that high-depth, long-read sequencing can probe SNPs, indels, homopolymeric tracts, and large-scale rearrangements in an unbiased fashion, and demonstrate that short deletions and homopolymer tract expansions arise spontaneously in A. flavus and other filamentous fungi.

papers.title: Cromosomal genomes assemblies of twelve sheep breeds
papers.abstract: The sheep research community benefits from a genome assembly that has been refined over the last 15 years. However, the rich diversity of sheep breeds suggests that a single individual genome is not enough to represent the species full genomic content. Third-generation sequencing technologies have recently made it possible to generate high quality assemblies that should enable to elucidate unique and/or complex phenotype determinisms depending on genetic structural variations. In the SeqOccin project, twelve breeds were selected to represent (mostly French) sheep genetic diversity: Basco-Bearnaise, Black Belly, Blanche du Massif Central, Corse, Ile de France, Lacaune, Manech Tete Noire, Noire du Velay, Ouessant, Rambouillet, Vendeen, Soay. High-molecular-weight DNA was extracted from blood samples and subjected to long read whole-genome sequencing. The reads were used to generate de novo assemblies and were aligned onto the public reference to call structural variants. PacBio HiFi and parental Illumina reads were used to assemble phased haplotypes of the Lacaune breed. For the other breeds, PacBio raw (CLR) or ONT reads were generated. Our work demonstrates the feasibility of assembling genomes with a reasonable amount of data and appropriate software packages, delivering one high-quality assembly and 11 standard sheep assemblies that pave the way for pangenome construction and structural variant functional studies.

papers.title: An iPSC-based experimental framework for investigating phenotypic variation associated with Jomon ancestry in the present-day Japanese population
papers.abstract: Ancestry-related genomic variation may contribute to phenotypic diversity. However, its cellular consequences remain difficult to evaluate. To address this, we developed a human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-based framework for investigating such phenotypes. We used the Japanese population as a model of Jomon-related and continental East Asian ancestry admixture. Jomon ancestry, estimated using the Jomon allele score (JAS), was associated with clinical measures, including renal-related traits and serum triglycerides in 34,152 Tohoku Medical Megabank participants. Peripheral blood mononuclear cell transcriptomics of donors from the upper and lower extremes of the JAS distribution (n = 10) suggested group-level differences in immune-related gene expression. To test whether the serum triglyceride association coincided with hepatic cellular phenotypes, we differentiated hiPSCs from these donors into hepatocyte-like cells. Neither intracellular triglycerides nor lipid-related gene expression differed between groups. These findings highlight the value of a genetically characterized hiPSC-based framework for investigating ancestry-associated phenotypes across cellular contexts.

papers.title: Scalable methylome-transcriptome profiling resolves clonal organization in human hematopoiesis
papers.abstract: Understanding human tissue maintenance and remodeling requires linking clonal ancestry to molecular state, yet scalable joint measurement remains challenging. Here, we introduce Droplet-MT and an integrated computational workflow for joint transcriptome and methylome profiling at ~10,000 cells per library. Methylation epimutations enable mutation-independent clonal reconstruction from high-coverage methylomes, while reference-based label transfer assigns cells to established clones at ~0.2% CpG coverage, reducing sequencing cost. Clone-aggregated somatic variants provide genetic annotation without additional single-cell genotyping. Across ~21,000 paired profiles from healthy blood and longitudinal acute myeloid leukemia, we resolved small and expanded clones with heterogeneous lineage output. In leukemia, the framework distinguished changes in malignant clonal abundance, state remodeling within persistent clones, and recovery of healthy polyclonal hematopoiesis. Malignant monocytes remained transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct from healthy and recovery-associated cells despite treatment-associated remodeling. Droplet-MT enables scalable analysis of human tissues by linking clonal organization with molecular state and retrospective genetic annotation.

papers.title: Matrix-Mechanical Genetic Susceptibility and Reduced Inflammatory and Immediate-Early Programs in Keratoconus
papers.abstract: Purpose. To determine which proposed keratoconus (KC) mechanisms carry its genetic susceptibility and how it relates to corneal structure, and which describe its corneal tissue. Methods. Six mechanism modules and two attribution sets (transforming growth factor-{beta} [TGF-{beta}] and canonical type-2 atopy) were tested for enrichment in three independent European KC genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and in GWAS of central corneal thickness (CCT) and corneal resistance factor (CRF), with colocalization at matrix loci. Tissue expression was pooled across nine arms from eight studies with control-source meta-regression; activator protein-1 (AP-1)/immediate-early regulatory activity was scored in 107 donors, spatial expression in 21, and serum responses in human and rabbit stromal cells. Results. Extracellular matrix (ECM) was the only module enriched in all three KC sources (P [≤] 5.46 x 10-) and for CCT, CRF, and thickness-independent CRF (P [≤] 2.07 x 10-). COL5A1 shared causal variants with CCT in all three sources (posterior probability 0.985-0.991), and FNDC3B and COL1A1 with CRF or its thickness-independent component (0.961-0.986). Pooled, KC corneas had lower general and corneal-local inflammatory and stress/immediate-early expression (log2 fold-change -0.97, -0.98, -0.82; P [≤] 0.049). In whole-cornea and stromal tissue, ECM expression reversed between postmortem-donor and pathological controls (log2 fold-change +0.36, -2.34), whereas inflammatory and TGF-{beta} programs were lower against both. AP-1/immediate-early regulatory activity was lower in four donor cohorts (Hedges' g -1.50) and stress/immediate-early expression in two spatial cohorts; serum raised immediate-early readouts in human and rabbit cells. Conclusions. KC combines matrix-mechanical genetic susceptibility with a low-inflammatory, low-immediate-early corneal state whose matrix expression direction depends on the control source. Because this susceptibility is genetically shared with corneal thickness and resistance, interventions on the inherited disease are judged by corneal structure and mechanics.

papers.title: Pooled progeny sequencing effectively estimates polyandry in species with large families
papers.abstract: Polyandry, multiple mating by females, both benefits females by increases genetic variation within families and provides an opportunity for sexual selection through sperm competition and cryptic female choice. Estimating polyandry in species with large clutches is challenging because genotyping all progeny individually can be impractical. We present a likelihood-based framework for estimating the number of sires and their relative contributions from the maternal genotype and pooled sequencing of entire progeny pools. The method evaluates the probability of observed pooled offspring read counts under alternative paternal genotype mixtures, accounting for Mendelian segregation and sampling variation from finite sequencing depth. We implement this framework for both biallelic SNPs and short-read mini-haplotype markers constructed from closely linked SNPs, which provide multi-allelic information comparable to traditional microsatellite markers. Simulations show that this approach accurately recovers sire number and sire contributions across a range of conditions. We then applied the method to 275 wild-caught Drosophila melanogaster females and their offspring from a Kansas population using 3,053 biallelic SNPs and 239 four-allele mini-haplotype markers. Estimates from the two marker sets were highly concordant, and combined analyses indicate that 57% of families were sired by a single male. These results demonstrate that pooled progeny sequencing provides an efficient genomic approach for estimating polyandry in species with large families.

papers.title: Systematic benchmark of demultiplexing workflows for direct RNA sequencing
papers.abstract: Direct RNA nanopore sequencing offers the capacity to directly profile native RNAs, enabling detection of diverse epitranscriptomic modifications based on current changes as the RNA passes through a pore. Innovations in chemistry, hardware and bioinformatic tools have increased sequencing capacity and accuracy, creating demand for sequencing multiple samples within individual runs. Two recent solutions enable barcoding and demultiplexing of samples, but independent comparisons of their performance is limited. Here we benchmark WarpDemuX and SeqTagger using orthogonal ground truths derived from species identity and matched IVT spike-ins across four RNA004 flow cells. Both achieve high demultiplexing precision but differ in their trade-offs in precision and retention. SeqTagger provided strong performance at its recommended settings, whilst WarpDemuX performance varied by model, barcode and read quality. IVT-derived score cutoffs allowed dataset-specific calibration and increased WarpDeMux assignment yield, although precision achieved on IVTs was not consistently reproduced in species reads. These results support matched IVTs as internal controls for guiding choice of demultiplexing settings, while demonstrating the need to validate demultiplexing precision in biological RNA populations.
